newsitem.title: RWANDA: Convicted Rwanda genocide leader waits for death.
newsitem.headline: Convicted Rwanda genocide leader waits for death.

text.p: A convicted ringleader of Rwanda's genocide, maintaining his innocence from death row, says he has little faith in the system of justice and believes he should have been tried as a political prisoner.
Froduald Karimira told a genocide court in January that he would willingly offer his life if it would mean an end to the hatreds that have torn the tiny Central African country apart.
"I cannot say I believe it would do any good," he told Reuters at the weekend.
He said he should be tried by a parallel United Nations genocide tribunal sitting at Arusha in Tanzania. It can deliver only life prison sentences as a maximum penalty.
"I am a politician and as a political prisoner I should be tried by the U.N. tribunal rather than a court here," Karamira said.
He said the last time he gave an interview criticising the justice system, he was locked for a month in solitary confinement.
Karamira's lawyer has appealed against the death sentence he received in February as a ringleader of the 1994 genocide in which an estimated 800,000 Tutsis were murdered along with moderate Hutus.

The court convicted Karamira for being a leader of the Interahamwe militia and making radio appeals for people to butcher their neighbours during three months of genocide ended by the takeover of Tutsi-led rebels who now rule the country.

Born a Tutsi, Karamira used a Rwandan custom to convert to the Hutu tribe, the majority that ruled Rwanda until 1994. The wealthy businessman was vice-president of the radical MDR-Power party under the Hutu-led government.
The vast majority of almost 100,000 people crammed into Rwanda's prisons are Hutus awaiting trial on accusations that they took part in the genocide at various levels.
Those like Karamira in the top of four categories face a mandatory death sentence if found guilty. So far 12 have been handed out.

"We still have to wait and see how fair the justice system is here, and we will be able to tell from the result of my appeal. I know I am not guilty, so if I am executed it will be clear that it is not fair," said Leonitas Ndikumwami, another prisoner sentenced to die.
Under Rwandan law, executions are carried out by firing squad away from public view.
Over 5,000 inmates at Kigali's central prison, awaiting trial or already sentenced, live packed on top of each other in cells built to hold under half their number.
"If you live here you don't notice the smell," said a mechanic who has spent two years there and has no idea when he will be brought to trial.
"Who knows? I could be here for 100 years," he added.
The lucky ones sleep in shifts in boxes stacked three high in the cells. The rest sleep on floors swabbed with disinfectant.
"What can anyone say about the conditions? You can see for yourself how we live," said Karamira, who was arrested at Ethiopia's Addis Ababa airport last June and extradited to Rwanda.
Rwanda has criticised the U.N. tribunal for its slow pace, poor investigations and inability to extradite the most important genocide ringleaders from exile abroad.
